summary: Jump search finds a target in a sorted array by jumping ahead in fixed-size blocks of about √n until it passes the target, then scanning linearly inside the last block. It takes O(√n) time: between linear and binary search.

sections.heading: Algorithm
bullets: Jump forward m positions at a time while a[min(step, n) - 1] < target.
When the block that could contain the target is found, scan it linearly.

sections.heading: Why √n
sections.body: With block size m, the cost is about n/m jumps plus up to m-1 linear steps. n/m + m is minimized when m = √n, giving roughly 2√n comparisons in the worst case.

sections.heading: Complexity
bullets: Ordering of speed: linear O(n) > jump O(√n) > binary O(log n).

sections.heading: When it makes sense
bullets: Jumping backward is expensive (e.g. tape or some storage), so jump search moves forward only except for one short scan.
Simpler to implement than binary search.
Otherwise binary search is almost always better on arrays.

sections.body: n = 16, step 4. Check a[3]=2 < 55, a[7]=13 < 55, a[11]=89 >= 55. Scan indices 8..11: 21, 34, 55 found at index 10. About 3 jumps plus 3 linear steps.

subtopics.title: Comparison with binary and interpolation search

bullets: Binary search: O(log n), needs random access.
Interpolation search: O(log log n) average on uniformly distributed keys, O(n) worst.

sections.body: Applying jump search inside each block (a multi-level jump) approaches binary search's cost. Exponential (galloping) search doubles the step until it overshoots, then binary searches the last interval.
On disks or tapes where sequential reads of a block are cheap and seeks are costly, skipping ahead in blocks and scanning one block mirrors how index structures like B-trees work.

bullets: Use integer sqrt and avoid floating error for large n.

takeaways: Jump ahead by √n, then scan the block linearly.
O(√n) time, O(1) space, sorted input only.
Faster than linear, slower than binary search.
Useful when moving backward is costly.
